subject: surgery
title: Femoropopliteal Bypass and Acute Limb Ischaemia

steps.tx: A graft carrying blood from the femoral artery to the popliteal artery past a blockage is a **femoropopliteal bypass**. The patients own leg vein is the preferred conduit because it stays open longest. It is used for long occlusions causing rest pain or tissue loss when balloon treatment cannot succeed.
steps.say: Femoropopliteal bypass uses the patients own vein to carry blood past long blockages causing tissue loss.

vis.alt: Peripheral arterial disease requiring bypass surgery.
vis.caption: Severe leg arterial disease needing bypass. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Sudden loss of blood flow to a limb threatening its survival is **acute limb ischaemia**. Causes include embolus from the heart and thrombosis on existing narrowing. Without flow restoration within hours, muscle and nerve die irreversibly. An embolus tends to lodge at the fork of the common femoral artery, and a normal other leg points away from chronic disease.
steps.say: Acute limb ischaemia suddenly threatens a limb, and flow must return within hours to save it.

steps.tx: The classic features of acute limb ischaemia are remembered as the **six Ps**. They are pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis and perishing cold. Loss of movement and sensation means the limb is in immediate danger. Paraesthesia and paralysis are late signs; once muscle is tender and stiff, the leg is usually unsalvageable.
steps.say: The six Ps describe acute limb ischaemia, and lost movement or sensation means immediate danger.

steps.tx: Surgical removal of a blood clot from an artery is **embolectomy**. A balloon catheter passed beyond the clot drags it out and restores flow. Heparin is given immediately when acute ischaemia is diagnosed to stop clot extension. Heparin should be given on diagnosis, before imaging, unless the leg is already being taken straight to theatre.
steps.say: Embolectomy drags clot out with a balloon catheter, and heparin starts immediately to stop extension.

steps.tx: Vein grafts need regular ultrasound surveillance after bypass, a programme of **graft surveillance**. Narrowings inside the graft are corrected before they cause thrombosis. Once a vein graft clots, results of rescue are much poorer. Scans at six weeks, then three, six and twelve months, catch the stenoses that appear in the first two years.
steps.say: Graft surveillance scans vein grafts so narrowings are corrected before thrombosis occurs.

steps.tx: When bypass is impossible and the limb cannot survive, removal of part of the leg is **major amputation**. Below knee amputation preserves walking potential far better than above knee. The level is chosen where blood supply can heal the stump. Energy spent walking with a below knee stump rises modestly, while above knee amputation can double it and loses most elderly patients their independence.
steps.say: Major amputation is chosen at a level that can heal when bypass cannot save the limb.

steps.tx: Compartment pressure rising after flow restoration can crush muscle, a complication called **compartment syndrome**. Reperfusion swells muscle inside tight fascial compartments. Emergency splitting of the compartments, fasciotomy, prevents permanent damage. Four compartment fasciotomy through medial and lateral incisions is the standard release for the calf.
steps.say: Compartment syndrome after reperfusion swells muscle in tight compartments and needs emergency fasciotomy.

steps.tx: A graft taken with its valves rendered useless by cutting them is an **in situ vein graft**. Leaving the vein in place preserves its wall nutrition. Valvulotomy lets blood flow the natural arterial direction. Cutting the valves risks narrowing the vein at each valve site, so completion angiography checks the whole conduit.
steps.say: In situ vein grafts leave the vein in place with valves cut to preserve wall nutrition.

steps.tx: Successful bypass depends more on outflow quality than graft length, the principle of **runoff**. A graft into a leg with open foot arteries stays patent far longer. Imaging runoff carefully is therefore essential before surgery. A single open tibial vessel to the foot can keep a graft working, while a blind ending graft usually clots early.
steps.say: Good runoff into foot arteries keeps bypass grafts open longer, so outflow imaging is essential.
